name: Barban
lead: Two Defranceschi families in 1945, and the parish where the surname still appears in Croatian records today.
body: Acta Croatica records surviving Defranceschi households in the Labin area at Barban into the present century — one of only four Croatian places where the name is still found.

name: Cerovlje
lead: The municipality Gologorica sits in today.
body: Included here because modern Croatian administration files Gologorica under Cerovlje, so civil records after 1945 are found under this name rather than the village's own.

name: Gologorica
lead: The family's documented seat. A De Franceschi house of 1711 still stands on the main square.
body: Municipality of Cerovlje, central Istria. Roman material has been found here, including a gravestone now in the Pazin museum. The parish church of Saints Peter and Paul carries Renaissance altars and a seventeenth-century baptismal font, and a small Romanesque chapel of the Blessed Virgin keeps fifteenth-century frescoes.
Carlo De Franceschi, the historian, was born here in 1809 — of modest landowners, in his own biographer's phrase, not of gentry. In October 1945 the village still held two Defranceschi families.

registers.note: The six undigitised books are the oldest — baptisms 1644–1763, marriages 1656–1781, burials 1646–1777.

name: Gračišće
lead: Eight household censuses across 150 years — the richest register series found anywhere in this project.
body: First recorded in 1199. Held by the Patriarch of Aquileia, then the counts of Gorizia, and from 1374 part of the Duchy of Pazin. Bishop Paskazije of Pićan consecrated the Gothic chapel here in 1486, in his own birthplace.
Glagolitic and Latin graffiti survive scratched into the chapel interior — Croatian, written in Croatian letters, inside a town the maps called Gallignana.

registers.note: Thirty-one of thirty-two books digitised. The status animarum give house-by-house listings roughly every twenty years.

name: Ližnjan
lead: Named by the existing family research as the origin of a line that went to the United States and Germany — and never worked in an archive.
body: The received account gives Ližnjan as one of four directions the family dispersed in, onward to the United States and Germany. No register work has been done on it, and the 1945 census records no Defranceschi household here — which does not disprove the line, but does mean it had already gone by then.
Twenty-four registers survive, baptisms from 1683. Only fourteen are digitised, the lowest proportion of any parish in this study.

name: Motovun
lead: One family in 1945 — and 121 of 122 registers digitised, the most complete series in the study.
body: A Venetian hill town whose registers open in 1586. If a link has to be traced through the western, Venetian half of Istria, this is the easiest parish in which to do it.

name: Pazin
lead: The county town. Its baptism register opens in 1582 — the oldest book in this study.
body: Capital of the Habsburg County of Pazin from the late fourteenth century, and so the administrative centre for every village in this archive's Istrian half. Carlo De Franceschi sat for Pisino in the Imperial Constituent Parliament of 1848; his son Camillo attended the German gymnasium here.
One hundred and thirty-nine registers survive, but the 1643–1882 baptismal series is largely undigitised.

name: Pićan
lead: The diocese Gologorica and Gračišće belonged to — but not the custodian of their registers.
body: A tiny bishopric with an outsized place in Istrian church history; in the Middle Ages both ecclesiastical and secular power at Pićan lay with the Patriarchs of Aquileia. Its own registers run from 1664 and are almost entirely digitised. One Defranceschi family was counted here in 1945.

name: Poreč
lead: Where Camillo De Franceschi was born in 1868, and where his father published L'Istria in 1879.
body: The Gologorica branch reached Poreč before it reached Crikvenica. It is also the seat of the diocesan archive that holds the later registers for half the parishes in this study.

name: Svetvinčenat
lead: One De Franceschi family in 1945 — spaced, not fused — and a baptism register opening in 1568.
body: One of only two places in Istria in 1945 where the surname is written in the spaced Venetian form. The other is Seghetto near Umag. Both are west of the old Habsburg border.

name: Umag
lead: The hamlet of Seghetto held one De Franceschi family in 1945. Every one of Umag's 128 registers is digitised.
body: The only parish in this study with a complete digitisation — 128 of 128 books, marriages from 1602. Whatever is here can be read from anywhere.

name: Vižinada
body: In the Motovun judicial district and the Poreč administrative district in 1945 — the Venetian side of the peninsula.

name: Vodnjan
lead: Twelve Defranceschi families in 1945 — by far the largest single concentration, and absent from the existing family narrative.
body: The 1945 cadastre counts twelve Defranceschi families at Vodnjan, against two at Gologorica and one at Gračišće. No line in the existing research accounts for them. Whether they are a branch of the Pazin-county family or an independent formation of the same very common patronymic is the second open question of this archive, after the Carnia–Istria link.

name: Čepić
lead: One family in 1945. The youngest register series in the study — nothing before 1782.
body: Recorded in the 1945 cadastre as Ceppici di Pòrtole, in the Motovun judicial district.

name: Crikvenica
lead: Named for a church: the Pauline monastery of 1412, in the deed that first records the name.
body: Nikola IV Frankopan gave the monastery to the Pauline fathers on 14 August 1412. The order stayed four hundred years, until Joseph II dissolved it in 1786, and for that whole time it was Vinodol's school, pharmacy and library.

A harbour came in 1877, a bathing beach in 1888, the first hotel in 1891 — a Vinodol village that became an Austrian seaside resort inside one lifetime. The Gologorica branch reached here by way of Poreč.

registers.note: No parish-level inventory is published. The whole Kvarner series sits in one collection — Zbirka matičnih knjiga s primorsko-goranskog područja, istočne Istre i Kvarnerskih otoka, HR-DARI-275 — 1,822 books over 40 linear metres, archivally arranged, only partially filmed and only partially available to the public. Six books were taken over from the Senj registry office in March 2018 and are held at the Senj collection centre. ARHiNET, the national catalogue that would carry the item list, did not resolve on any attempt.

name: Senj
lead: An Uskok garrison on the Habsburg Military Frontier — never Italian, unlike Istria.
body: Taken over by the Habsburgs in 1522 as a state-controlled Militärgrenze, and from the 1530s the base of the Uskoks, the refugee raiders who fought the Ottomans and Venice until an agreement between Habsburg and Venice expelled them in 1617. The Nehaj fortress was built by the Uskok captain Ivan Lenković in 1558.
Records for Senj fall to the State Archives in Rijeka, whose remit covers Primorje-Gorski Kotar plus the city of Senj. That inventory is not yet mapped.

name: Mione
lead: A hundred and thirty people at 710 metres — and the Italian end of a documented migration into Istria.
body: First written on 15 June 1185, when Odolrico called Gusetto, Strabo, and Vecellone, son-in-law of Giovanni da Mione, received concessions from Domenico, abbot of Moggio. An independent comune until 1871, now a frazione of Ovaro in the Canale di Gorto.

A stone above the village, at some 1,600 metres, carries Venetic inscriptions — this valley was a route long before it was a parish. From the parishes of Ovaro and Luincis a long series of weavers took the road into Istria; the documents become numerous in the seventeenth century and frequent in the eighteenth.

registers.note: Mione is listed as its own civil registration unit for 1806–1815, alongside Luincis, Liariis, Muina and Ovasta.
